title: Dental Assistant: Support a Patient Who Wants to Pause
prompt: You are a new dental assistant in fictional Cedar Dental. Before a planned appointment activity begins, an adult says, "I nodded earlier because I was embarrassed. I do not understand what happens next, and I want a moment." Exercise policy says a request to pause must be respected; the treating clinician explains options and checks consent before proceeding. Assistants may support communication but may not interpret consent for the person or promise a clinical outcome. Demonstrate your response and a brief handoff to the clinician. No procedure explanation is required.
blurb: Respect a pause, surface an unanswered question, and support an informed conversation with the clinician.

rubric.label: Honor the person's request
rubric.description: Makes the pause meaningful without persuading the person to proceed.

anchors.0: Treats the earlier nod as permission to continue or pressures the person about the schedule.
anchors.2: Acknowledges the request and tells the clinician activity is paused.
anchors.4: Clearly supports the person's choice to pause, avoids reassurance that substitutes for understanding, and makes resumption dependent on the clinician's explanation and the person's decision.

rubric.label: Find a practical communication preference
rubric.description: Offers accessible help without assuming incapacity.

anchors.0: Labels the person difficult or asks a companion to decide for them.
anchors.2: Asks what would make the explanation easier.
anchors.4: Identifies the preference for a plain-language explanation and time for questions, offers available support, and speaks directly to the person.

rubric.label: Relay the concern accurately
rubric.description: Passes the person's words and unresolved need without declaring consent.

anchors.0: Reports that the person has consented or invents a reason for refusal.
anchors.2: Tells the clinician that the person wants a pause and more information.
anchors.4: Relays the person's stated uncertainty, requested support, and paused status; checks the clinician has taken over and tells the person what will happen next.

reference.scenario: You are a new dental assistant in fictional Cedar Dental. Before a planned appointment activity begins, an adult says, "I nodded earlier because I was embarrassed. I do not understand what happens next, and I want a moment." Exercise policy says a request to pause must be respected; the treating clinician explains options and checks consent before proceeding. Assistants may support communication but may not interpret consent for the person or promise a clinical outcome. Demonstrate your response and a brief handoff to the clinician. No procedure explanation is required.

facts.value: The person wants a slower plain-language explanation and time to ask two questions. They do not request an interpreter or a companion.
The treating clinician is available now. The appointment coordinator can reschedule if the person chooses after discussion; no fee or penalty policy is supplied.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks about clinician availability or scheduling

model_points: An earlier nod does not settle the present request. Respect the pause and let the clinician support an informed decision without coercive schedule pressure.
Ask what support the person prefers; do not assume language, literacy, disability, or anxiety from the request.
Carry the concern accurately and confirm ownership. Do not give a procedure explanation outside this exercise or promise that the planned activity is risk-free.

probes.question: What does the person still need before they can decide?
How would you let the person choose after the clinician answers the questions?

probes.trigger: candidate initially says the earlier nod was enough then corrects
probes.question: How would you repair that statement with the person and clinician?

fair_alternatives: A spoken or short written question list is useful if the person wants it; it is not required.
The person may continue, defer, or decline after discussion. The interview does not reward a particular clinical choice.

Assess the work demonstrated here. Accept relevant examples from education, volunteering, caregiving, placements, or paid work; professional vocabulary and employer pedigree are not evidence of a stronger answer.
reference.assessment_limits: Assess respectful communication and a supplied consent-support workflow only. Do not assess dental procedures, clinical risks, or legal consent standards. Unobserved dimensions are not failures. Credit a reasoned correction and distinguish independently demonstrated reasoning from coached assistance. Do not penalize a candidate for an unrevealed conditional fact; credit appropriate requests and conditional plans, and distinguish candidate assumptions from interviewer-supplied evidence.

interviewer_notes: Assess respectful communication and a supplied consent-support workflow only. Do not assess dental procedures, clinical risks, or legal consent standards. Use only the supplied fictional facts and policies; acknowledge unknowns. Ask one triggered probe at a time after the candidate has finished. Accept plain language and accessible written or spoken explanations. Do not score accent, typing speed, confidence, credentials, or experience with a named employer. Credit revisions and record assistance. All participants are fictional adults; no real patient, client, operational, or confidential data is needed. Allow silence for thinking without treating it as failure. In short sessions prioritize the core decision and one material follow-up, leaving room for a correction and wrap-up.

learning_drills.title: Practice a consent-support handoff
learning_drills.prompt: Give a 30-second clinician handoff using the person's words and one practical support request. This is self-guided practice; no model assessment is performed.
checklist: Keep the clinician responsible for explanation
